q: In a period, the properties of transition elements are very similar in contrast to those of s-block and p-block elements.
e: True. In a period, the properties of transition elements are very similar in contrast to those of s-block and p-block elements. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: In a period, the properties of transition elements are very different in contrast to those of s-block and p-block elements.
e: False. Across a transition series the properties change only gradually and stay similar. That is the contrast with the sharp s- and p-block jumps.

q: Many of the properties of transition elements are similar, but they are very different from other metals in Groups I and II (alkali and alkaline earth metals).

q: Nickel and copper do not react with water, or catch fire in the air (oxygen), unlike sodium.
e: True. Nickel and copper do not react with water, or catch fire in the air (oxygen), unlike sodium. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Nickel and copper react vigorously with water, or catch fire in the air (oxygen), like sodium.
e: False. Nickel and copper are unreactive compared with sodium. They do not catch fire in air or attack water vigorously.

q: In general, transition metals do not corrode readily in the atmosphere.
e: True. In general, transition metals do not corrode readily in the atmosphere. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Iron is an exception; it rusts easily.
e: True. Iron is an exception; it rusts easily. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Iron is an exception; it does not rust easily.
e: False. Iron rusts readily in damp air. That easy corrosion is a central fact about iron, not an exception against rusting.

q: Iron combined with non-metal carbon produces an alloy called steel.
e: True. Iron combined with non-metal carbon produces an alloy called steel. An alloy is a mixture of metals with useful combined properties.

q: Iron combined with non-metal silicon produces an alloy called steel.
e: False. Steel is iron with carbon, not silicon as the defining partner. Silicon steels exist, but the basic alloy named steel is Fe plus C.

q: Most transition elements form coloured compounds.
e: True. Most transition elements form coloured compounds. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Most transition elements form white compounds.
e: False. Most transition-metal compounds are coloured. White or colourless ions usually have empty or full d subshells, like Sc3+ and Zn2+.

q: The Groups 1 and II metals form white compounds.
e: True. The Groups 1 and II metals form white compounds. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Most of them can form ions with different charges.

q: Most transition elements can form complex ions.

q: Transition elements typically have incompletely filled d orbitals or readily give rise to ions with partially filled d orbitals.
e: True. Transition elements typically have incompletely filled d orbitals or readily give rise to ions with partially filled d orbitals. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Transition elements typically have completely filled d orbitals or readily give rise to ions with completely filled d orbitals.
e: False. Typical transition behaviour needs incomplete d orbitals. Completely filled d10 is the zinc-group case.

q: Transition elements exhibit variable oxidation states.
e: True. Transition elements exhibit variable oxidation states. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: The elements in the middle of the series exhibit more oxidation states than those to the left or right.
e: True. The elements in the middle of the series exhibit more oxidation states than those to the left or right. Oxidation state tracks how oxidised an atom is; transition metals often show several values.

q: The elements in the middle of the series exhibit fewer oxidation states than those to the left or right.
e: False. The middle of the series shows the most oxidation states. Mn and Cr are the classic many-state examples.

q: Iron ($_{26}\text{Fe}$) is known to form oxidation states from +2 to +6, with iron(II) and iron(III) being the most common.
e: True. Iron (26Fe) is known to form oxidation states from +2 to +6, with iron(II) and iron(III) being the most common. Oxidation state tracks how oxidised an atom is; transition metals often show several values.

q: Iron ($_{26}\text{Fe}$) is known to form oxidation states from +1 to +5, with iron(I) and iron(II) being the most common.
e: False. The common iron states are +2 and +3. Iron(I) is not the everyday chemistry of iron.

q: The highest oxidation state is +7 for manganese ($_{25}\text{Mn}$).
e: True. The highest oxidation state is +7 for manganese (25Mn). Oxidation state tracks how oxidised an atom is; transition metals often show several values.

q: The highest oxidation state is +6 for manganese ($_{25}\text{Mn}$).
e: False. Manganese reaches +7, as in permanganate. +6 is not its highest state.

q: The ions of chromium, manganese, and iron have the highest oxidation states, +6, +7, and +6, respectively.
e: True. The ions of chromium, manganese, and iron have the highest oxidation states, +6, +7, and +6, respectively. Oxidation state tracks how oxidised an atom is; transition metals often show several values.

q: In contrast, vanadium and chromium ions with the lowest oxidation state of +2 are good reducing agents, such as vanadium(II) ion ($\text{V}^{2+}$) and chromium(II) ion ($\text{Cr}^{2+}$).
e: True. In contrast, vanadium and chromium ions with the lowest oxidation state of +2 are good reducing agents, such as vanadium(II) ion (V2+) and chromium(II) ion (Cr2+). Oxidation state tracks how oxidised an atom is; transition metals often show several values.

q: In contrast, vanadium and chromium ions with the lowest oxidation state of +2 are good oxidising agents, such as vanadium(II) ion ($\text{V}^{2+}$) and chromium(II) ion ($\text{Cr}^{2+}$).
e: False. V2+ and Cr2+ are reducing agents; they want to be oxidised. Low oxidation state means they donate electrons.

q: Because of their greater nuclear attraction force, divalent ions of $\text{Co}^{2+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ are poor reducing agents.
e: True. Because of their greater nuclear attraction force, divalent ions of Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, and Zn2+ are poor reducing agents. The because-clause is the chemical reason that makes the statement hold.

q: Because of their weaker nuclear attraction force, divalent ions of $\text{Co}^{2+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ are strong reducing agents.
e: False. Those later divalent ions are not strong reducing agents. High-oxidation-state species on the left, such as MnO4-, are the strong oxidants.

q: Transition metals usually have their highest oxidation states in compounds with high electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine.
e: True. Transition metals usually have their highest oxidation states in compounds with high electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Transition metals usually have their highest oxidation states in compounds with low electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine.
e: False. Highest states appear with highly electronegative partners, oxygen and fluorine. Low electronegativity would not stabilise a high metal oxidation state.

q: The transition metal compounds form coloured ions in an aqueous solution because they absorb part of the visible light and transmit the complement colour.
e: True. The transition metal compounds form coloured ions in an aqueous solution because they absorb part of the visible light and transmit the complement colour. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: The transition metal compounds form coloured ions in an aqueous solution because they emit part of the visible light and absorb the complement colour.
e: False. The ion absorbs some visible wavelengths. You see the complementary colour that is not absorbed, not light the ion is emitting.

q: $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions are colourless because $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ion has completely empty d orbitals, and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has completely filled d orbitals.
e: True. Sc3+ and Zn2+ ions are colourless because Sc3+ ion has completely empty d orbitals, and Zn2+ has completely filled d orbitals. An orbital is a region of space where an electron is likely to be found.

q: $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions are highly coloured because $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ion has completely empty d orbitals, and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has completely filled d orbitals.
e: False. Empty d0 and full d10 ions are colourless. There is no d-d absorption, so Sc3+ and Zn2+ are not highly coloured.

q: The magnetic properties of a transition metal can be determined by examining the paired or unpaired electrons in $(n-1)d$ orbitals.
e: True. The magnetic properties of a transition metal can be determined by examining the paired or unpaired electrons in (n-1)d orbitals. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: If the electrons are unpaired then it is a paramagnetic substance.
e: True. If the electrons are unpaired then it is a paramagnetic substance. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: If the electrons are unpaired then it is a diamagnetic substance.
e: False. Unpaired electrons make a substance paramagnetic. Diamagnetic means all electrons are paired.

q: If the electrons are paired, then it is a diamagnetic substance.
e: True. If the electrons are paired, then it is a diamagnetic substance. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: According to the electronic configurations of the 3d series transition elements, scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, and manganese are paramagnetic substances whereas copper and zinc are diamagnetic substances.
e: True. According to the electronic configurations of the 3d series transition elements, scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, and manganese are paramagnetic substances whereas copper and zinc are diamagnetic substances. q: According to the electronic configurations of the 3d series transition elements, scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, and manganese are diamagnetic substances whereas copper and zinc are paramagnetic substances.
e: False. Early 3d atoms have unpaired d electrons and are paramagnetic. Zinc is d10 and diamagnetic; copper atoms are paramagnetic.

q: Most of the transition elements and their compounds are paramagnetic.
e: True. Most of the transition elements and their compounds are paramagnetic. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Substances that are attracted very strongly by the applied magnetic field are said to be ferromagnetic.
e: True. Substances that are attracted very strongly by the applied magnetic field are said to be ferromagnetic. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Substances that are repelled very strongly by the applied magnetic field are said to be ferromagnetic.
e: False. Strong repulsion is diamagnetism. Ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted and can stay magnetised.

q: Iron, cobalt, and nickel are ferromagnetic substances.
e: True. Iron, cobalt, and nickel are ferromagnetic substances. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Iron, cobalt, and copper are ferromagnetic substances.
e: False. The ferromagnetic trio is iron, cobalt, and nickel. Copper is not ferromagnetic.

q: Transition metals are widely used at the industrial level due to their catalytic properties.
e: True. Transition metals are widely used at the industrial level due to their catalytic properties. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: Iron and vanadium are the most important catalysts.
e: True. Iron and vanadium are the most important catalysts. A catalyst changes rate by opening a new path and is not used up overall.

q: Iron is used as a catalyst in the manufacture of ammonia (Haber process).
e: True. Iron is used as a catalyst in the manufacture of ammonia (Haber process). A catalyst changes rate by opening a new path and is not used up overall.

q: Iron is used as a catalyst in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (Contact process).
e: False. The Contact process uses V2O5. Iron is the Haber-process catalyst for ammonia.

q: Vanadium is used in the form of vanadium(V) oxide ($\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$) in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (Contact process).
e: True. Vanadium is used in the form of vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (Contact process). pH is the negative log of [H+], so a smaller pH means a more acidic solution.

q: Vanadium is used in the form of vanadium(V) oxide ($\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$) in the manufacture of ammonia (Haber process).
e: False. V2O5 is the Contact-process catalyst for sulphuric acid. Haber ammonia uses iron.

q: Nickel is used as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of alkenes.
e: True. Nickel is used as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of alkenes. A catalyst changes rate by opening a new path and is not used up overall.

q: Nickel is used as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of alkanes.
e: False. Nickel hydrogenates alkenes, turning C=C into C-C. Alkanes are already saturated, so they are not the usual feedstock.

q: Titanium(IV) chloride ($\text{TiCl}_4$) is used for the manufacturing of high-density polyethene in industries.
e: True. Titanium(IV) chloride (TiCl4) is used for the manufacturing of high-density polyethene in industries. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Titanium(IV) chloride ($\text{TiCl}_4$) is used for the manufacturing of low-density polyethene in industries.
e: False. TiCl4 is a Ziegler-Natta catalyst for high-density polyethene. LDPE is made by a high-pressure free-radical process.
